that Bill C-209, an Act respecting the execution of mass murderers, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I certainly hope that this Bill will pass second reading stage and go to committee. I believe it deserves that treatment.
This Bill is necessary because the Criminal Code of Canada fails to provide for the proper punishment of mass murderers, sometimes called serial murderers. The continued existence of mass murderers, or serial murderers, is a constant source of fear to Canadians in general and particularly to women and children.
The Bill provides for the execution of anyone who deliberately plans and kills 10 or more human beings and is found guilty beyond the shadow of a doubt.
One such murderer is Clifford Robert Olson. No one can deny that the murder of these girls and boys was not deliberately planned and carried out in cold blood. Let me outline this murder spree of Clifford Robert Olson. He had no conscience and killed simply for kicks. The first murder was that of Christine N. Weller. Olson took her to Richmond on November 17, 1980, and killed her with multiple stab wounds. Her murder, like that of all the others that followed, was planned and deliberate.
Five months later, Clifford Olson took Colleen Daignault to Surry and killed her. Her murder was also planned and deliberate. The cause of her death was skull fracture.
Five days later, Clifford Robert Olson took Daryn Todd Johnsrude to Deroche on April 21, 1981, and caused his unlawful death. The cause of death was skull fractures.

December 13, 1984
Execution of Mass Murderers Act
The fifth murder was that of Ada Anita Court, which took place just one month after the murder of Daryn. On June 21, 1981, Clifford Robert Olson took her to Agassiz and caused her death. The cause was strangulation.
Eleven days later, Clifford Robert Olson took Simon Patrick Partington, a nine-year old boy, to Richmond and killed him. The cause was strangulation.
The next murder took place 28 days later. Sandra Lynn Wolfsteiner disappeared on May 19, and finally Olson admitted that he killed her.
The next murder was seven days after that. Clifford Robert Olson took Judy Elizabeth Kozma to Agassiz on July 9 and caused her unawful death by multiple stab wounds.
Just two days later Clifford Robert Olson took Raymond Lawrence King to Agassiz. He killed him on July 23, 1981. The cause of death was skull fractures.
Again, just two days later, this man-if one can call him a man-took Sigrun Charlotte to Richmond and killed her on July 5. The cause of death was skull fractures. Just two days later, Clifford Robert Olson took Terri Lynn Carson to Agassiz and killed her by strangulation on July 27, 1981.
On July 21, just three days after the murder of Terri, he took Louise M. Chartrand to Whistler and killed her. The cause of her death was skull fractures.
Those are the 11 murders that this man carried out in that short period of time. In the month of July alone, he killed five people in cold blood. The evidence indicates that many of them were put through sordid degradation. The evidence is sufficient to indicate that at least some of these people faced sexual abuse and degradation before they were murdered.
I will deal with his sentence in a few moments. The first question I want to raise is whether Olson can be rehabilitated. In his 42 years of misspent life, Olson compiled a list of crimes which kept him behind the bars for the best part of 25 years. He committed one crime after another, and then capped it all with the murder spree of at least 11 young people. He now openly brags that he killed several others in the United States, for which he has not yet been convicted.
Perhaps the words of the wife of Olson can give an insight into the kind of man we are dealing with. She told the Supreme Court hearing that she was married to "an animal who terrorized me". She also told of nightmares that haunted her before her husband was caught in which the ghost of the murdered nine-year old boy, Simon Partington, begged her to help him. Whether it was a ghost or a dream, she sincerely felt that this young child was begging for help while her husband was brutalizing and killing him. She went on to say, "Oh, I hate him-I've hated him since the night he held a knife to my throat".
Robert Shantz, Olson's lawyer at one time, said that Clifford Olson is "conscienceless creep" who should be executed. He went on to say that, "There isn't anything that current medical science can do to change that fellow. You let him out and he is likely to have three more kids killed". This has been
verified and confirmed by other highly trained psychologists. I ask the House: can he be rehabilitated?
First, Olson has no remorse for what he did. He laughed when he was collecting the money for the people he had murdered. Second, most experts say that, without a conscience, a serial killer cannot be reformed. Dr. Morrison, an American psychiatrist, said, "They are untreatable, unrehabilitatable, and uncontrollable". He went on to say that they can put on a good act but they cannot be reformed.
I submit that there is as much chance of Clifford Robert Olson being rehabilitated as the proverbial snowball staying a snowball in Hades.
Second, is it proper to try Olson a second time? This is an important question. Some people have raised the objection that this would be retroactive legislation which violates the fundamental principles of justice. Let me give you one or two instances. Adolf Eichmann was executed for crimes he committed prior to 1945 by laws which could not have been in existence prior to 1948 because Israel did not exist prior to 1948. The crimes he committed were so terrible there was no question that he should have been executed. He was. War criminals who were tried by army courts and who were not punished sufficiently were then tried by civilian courts and punished. Other war criminals were executed years after they had committed their crimes. There is an exception to every rule, and it is accepted generally by people around the world. When the reason is strong enough, the exception is made. Here we have a man who murdered 11 young people, laughs about it, and wants to profit by it. Twenty-five years in prison is not adequate. He has special guards, special protection, and special privileges. He watches television. He write letters, I do not know how many, with the dirtiest and most profane language 1 have ever read. The taxpayers of Canada are paying to keep a man like that alive.
Third, who will be responsible if Olson does escape or is eventually paroled? Not a boy or a girl on his street would be safe. He gets his kicks from killing boys and girls. Would those of you who think he should not be executed have him live beside your sons and daughters who have small children? Would you want him next door to you?
Retroactive legislation has beneficial side effects because if the possibility of retroactive legislation had been publicized, anyone who wanted to commit a murder today could no longer be absolutely certain that he will not be executed tomorrow. Who knows how many lives might have been saved from potential murderers because this Bill was on the Order Paper?
Next I want to look at the experience in one other country, namely, China. China, which we think is so primitive, established the death penalty for serious crimes. It included homicide, rape, robbery, explosions, and other activities. The report states that two months after taking this hard line, that is that people who committed crimes and were found guilty would be executed, crime fell to its lowest level in years, dropping 46.7 per cent one month and 11.5 per cent more the next month.
December 13, 1984

Death is a deterrent. Everybody wants to live. Very few want to die. Death is certainly a deterrent. It is certainly a deterrent when a man has committed a number of crimes and is then executed. He will not commit any more crimes. Had Clifford Olson been executed after he murdered the first girl, Christine Ann Weller, there would be ten fine young people alive today, but he was not executed.
I want to outline a few comments that I have in a thick file of letters from people all across Canada. One deals with the last point I want to make. People are urging that this Bill be passed. In the last session of Parliament I tabled more than 10,000 petitions from people across Canada who said that Clifford Robert Olson has no right to live. The punishment given to him is not adequate. Here are some comments. Here is what one person said, "It might be a good idea to let Olson mingle with the other prisoners". You know what would happen if they did that, Mr. Speaker? Why should the state make criminals carry out what is the state's duty? Other comments are: "Why should the taxpayer protect him? The children he killed were never given any protection and in a society where we thought they did not require it. Well, those children are rotting in their graves. Justice is a joke in Canada. A life sentence is a farce. These murderers are out in five years. He is dehumanized and should be treated in the same method given a mad dog suffering with rabies".
Fourth, execution works in other places as a deterrent. I have given the instance of China. By law, Olson's sentence means that no request for parole may be considered until he has served at least 25 years. The judge recommended that he not be permitted to have parole then, but strange things happen in our land. Olson escaped before from a maximum security prison. He may escape again. If he is executed, he will not be escaping or killing any more boys or girls. What if he does escape? I do not want the blood of the boys and girls on my coat-tails. I do not want the blood of the boys and girls he has already killed on my coat-tails. The man should be executed.
Some people have said to me that they do not believe in capital punishment because the wrong man may be executed. But there is no chance of the wrong man being executed in this case. It will be Clifford Robert Olson.
I want to close with a comment that came to me from somewhere in Canada, I forget where. The person said, "The man continues to make a mockery of our judicial system. He is still front page news because of our obsession with the money that was paid to him to uncover his victims, while his victims' ghosts are screaming in our apathetic ears for justice to be done". This person went on to say, "I hope they continue to scream. I hope they scream so loud that we are awakened from our self-serving lives determined to right the wrongs for which our neighbours' children have already suffered the consequences".
I have no hesitation whatsoever in moving that this Bill be read a second time and that Clifford Robert Olson be executed.
Execution of Mass Murderers Act

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has raised a very important question. However, Bill C-209 respecting the execution of mass murders only deals with part of the problem in my opinion. I think that its scope should be extended.
What I do not understand is that although our constituents have made this a priority issue the Government opposite is showing no leadership on the question of the death penalty. When I was elected in 1979, one of the first things I did was to ask my constituents this question in a householder mailing: Do you agree with a return of the death penalty? 85 per cent of them answered yes. This was the opinion of my constituents in 1979. They were for a return of the death penalty. Each week,
1 receive letters from people throughout the country. In nine out of ten cases, people favour a return of the death penalty.
In terms of human tragedy, we often forget those who are the real victims. It is not only the one who is killed whose rights are violated, but all those around him who love him, his father, his mother, his sons, his daughters, his brothers and his sisters, and the spouse who go through a very harrowing and even traumatic experience.
The major problem revolves around the application of the law. If our institutions are unable to keep convicts in jail and if the convicts continue to escape, our correctional system should be reformed. How many times do we read in the newspapers that people on parole have committed another crime? How many times do we hear that they have committed acts of violence and even murders? The Government should have the courage, first of all, to submit the issue of the death penalty to a free vote in this House, and second, to review our parole system.
Mr. Speaker, I know that other Members want to speak, but in closing, I could perhaps suggest that we consider having a national referendum on the death penalty. I often have the feeling that some Members in this House are saying that their constituents want the death penalty, but that they themselves are against it. Are we here to represent our constituents or not? For my part, I would vote for a return of the death penalty for first degree murder.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to place a few remarks on the record concerning Bill C-209 in the name of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). The entire subject of capital punishment is a very emotional one, yet it is important to recognize, as did the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay), that we have to deal with this matter in a reasonable manner, not simply be caught up in an emotional stampede. I am opposed to capital punishment in principle. I am not simply opposed to this Bill, but I am opposed to capital punishment for four reasons.

December 13, 1984
Execution of Mass Murderers Act
First, capital punishment tends to be class legislation. People who are well to do are able to afford lawyers. They can go the whole route in terms of postponing trials, obtaining extensions and appeals, and bringing in witnesses. The route is something which helps many more people with money to be acquitted than people who do not have money. In the end, people who do not have money are executed, and those who have money are acquitted much more often.
Second-and the Hon. Member referred to it in his speech-there is always the possibility of convicting the innocent. For example, Donald Marshall of Nova Scotia served 11 years in prison for a murder which he did not commit. If we are to be consistent, we have to recognize that if we apply capital punishment for any reason, there is always the possibility that the innocent will be convicted.
Third, capital punishment is not a deterrent. Studies have been conducted in States in the U.S. which have capital punishment and are adjacent to States where capital punishment does not exist. These studies have shown that the rate of murder does not vary significantly. In fact, violence begets violence. If we want to encourage a violent society, perhaps returning to capital punishment is one way of doing it.
The fourth reason is a very important one. Juries tend not to convict when they know that a human life depends upon their decision. When they know that what they decide will result in whether another human being lives or dies, they are very reluctant to convict someone.
A number of Private Members' Bills have been given first reading in this session. Of the bills submitted, I believe the present one is perhaps the most objectionable from a legal point of view because it attempts to apply capital punishment in a retroactive manner. It is specifically designed to deal with a single individual. I agree with the Hon. Member that Clifford Robert Olson is a most odious individual. There is no one in the House who would want to defend such a person. As a person who opposes capital punishment in principle, I would go as far as to say that if anyone has forfeited his or her right to life, it would be a person like Clifford Robert Olson. However, I do not think that this is any reason for us to provide a retroactive law applying capital punishment. It is a repugnant principle in law.
The Hon. Member is aware of the concerns within his Party about applying a retroactive 25 per cent back-in under the National Energy Program. In that instance we are talking about money, and they oppose it in principle. They find it most repugnant. However, the Hon. Member is willing to take a life by passing a retroactive law. I think that illustrates the legal fallacy and the objectionable legal quality of the Bill which he is proposing.
Perhaps capital punishment gives society the feeling that we are doing something about a problem when we are not, or that we are dealing adequately with the situation when we are not.
It was revealing that when the news of the Olson murders first broke several years ago, a psychologist pointed out that there were five or six young people, children, in British
Columbia at that time who, he believed, had the potential to act in the same manner as Clifford Olson. He was saying this at the same time that British Columbia was shutting down facilities to help such children.
Why are we not demanding diagnostic or treatment facilities for children in crisis so that they have some possibility of growing up and living normal and decent lives? We have to attack this kind of problem at its roots instead of waiting until we have a crisis, saying that we will take the life of a person we all find objectionable and feeling that somehow we are dealing with the problem.
In conclusion, I find this Bill to be a most objectionable one. It is a subject with which all of us have a great deal of difficulty dealing. I do not believe the Hon. Member's measures will in any way deal with the matter in an adequate fashion. People such as Clifford Olson have to be kept in permanent confinement. There is no doubt about that. I agree with the Solicitor General that we have to deal with this subject in a reasonable way. We should not be following blind emotion.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to second this Bill. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), has my support for the second reading of Bill C-209, an Act respecting the execution of mass murderers. I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak in favour of the Bill.
It is very important that we have a concrete definition of mass murderers before we begin to discuss the various concerns and solutions. According to the Oxford Concise Dictionary, murder is the unlawful killing of a human being with malice aforethought, that is premeditated and ill-meaning. Mass means relating to large numbers of persons or things or on a large scale. Therefore, we can safely say that a mass murderer is one who unlawfully kills a large number of human beings, having previously intended to do so.
In this category we must include not only those people who unlawfully kill a number of people at one time, but those who murder several people over a period of time. The latter is often called a serial murderer, and they definitely fall into the mass murder category because they are personally responsible for taking several lives.
At this time I would like to add that it is my opinion that one murder is one too many. Anyone responsible for the murder of two or more people is a mass murderer, in my judgment. I would like to point out that there is a very important distinction between those people who murder once and those who are responsible for several tragic deaths. While murder in any form is deplorable, the one-time murderer has often committed the crime in a moment of passion.
May I stress again that I do not condone that action. Murder is murder, no matter what the circumstances. My point is that the one-time murderer usually acts without malicious intent. It is in a moment of passion or emotion that
December 13, 1984

he or she decides to revenge or benefit himself or herself, or it may be a case of fear, fear of being caught in the act of committing another wrong. It is rarely an act that has been thought out and it is rarely repeated.
The mass murder or serial murder is a completely different case. If possible, it is even more deplorable. It is a repeated deliberate action not only to harm, but to destroy another life. This is the murderer who kills again and again and feels no remorse for his or her actions. It is carefully thought out and usually cleverly executed. A pattern develops and the murderer chooses similar circumstances and methods for each death.
What makes this type of murder absolutely unbearable is the complete lack of respect given to the life of others, not only once, but several times over. What words can we possibly use to explain how terrible this crime is? We need only look at the victims and their surviving families to come to a realization of the disaster and chaos such a murderer brings to our citizens. There is an added dimension of pain and heartbreak to the family of a victim of a mass murder. The knowledge that the person responsible for killing a loved one has done so before to other families, and may do so again, is especially frightening. We need only talk to family members who have had a mother, father, brother, sister or child callously murdered. The pain is doubled because you know you are not alone in your suffering. Other families are experiencing the same pain.
There may be strength in numbers, but this is a terrible bond to have with others. So they suffer and wonder why their family, why their daughter, son, sister, brother, mother or father? Why indeed. It is hard to understand how a mass murderer, or serial murderer, picks his victims. There is rarely any connection between the victims of a serial murderer. There is no logical process by which the murderer singles out his prey. In most murders of this kind the victims are vulnerable single people, children out alone, elderly people on their own, women out by themselves.
Another similarity is that the victims are nearly always strangers to the murderer. They have to be strangers because the murderer needs the thrill of the chase. He chooses someone, be it male or female, who can be caught alone. Sometimes the killer seeks to gain his victim's trust, only so he can monstrously betray it. Such murders are monstrous. The actual killing is often sadistic and the murderer thrives upon the terror he induces in his unfortunate victim.
The question is, what can we do to stop or prevent such horrible crimes like these from continuing? Can we deter people from considering and committing this sort of murder? I strongly believe that we can, and more, that we must. We have a responsibility to our citizens and ourselves to make sure that we do just that. We have the technology and know-how to do so many incredible things. Yet for too long we have not implemented the one sure way to prevent the massive loss of human lives that occurs when mass murder takes place.
I am referring to the deterrent of capital punishment. While many mass or serial murderers put little or no value on another's life, they are still very concerned with the preservation of their own. The knowledge that, by taking the lives of
Execution of Mass Murderers Act
others, one may lose one's own life is definitely something that would make one stop and think. It would force the potential mass murderer to think twice, once about his own life and the second time about another person's life.
Most of us would never really consider taking someone else's life. If the possibility of losing our own life was a very real and probable result from taking another's life, I am confident that an individual would be deterred from murder the first time.
As I mentioned earlier, while murderers may have little or no concern for their victim's life, they are very protective of their own. Most actions are based on a strong desire to protect and affirm one's own self. In order to present the mass murderer with a very real deterrent, we must concentrate on the one aspect of his life that does mean something to him, that is his own life. I am not talking about a vengeful action in taking a murderer's life.
I would also like to mention that hanging is not the only method available for the implementation of capital punishment. I sincerely believe that we can be more humane in our methods. The purpose of capital punishment is not to take revenge. It is to be used as a deterrent to prevent a potential murderer from becoming an actual one. I am talking about giving a clear choice to the potential murderer. If an individual decides to kill, then he should be held responsible with his own life. We must ensure that that choice is made clear to the murderer. It is his choice.
We have a responsibility to uphold our end of the bargain. Our parents taught us values and the lessons of life by warning us of the consequences our actions would bring. We must ensure that potential murderers understand that they will be asked to atone for their actions.
I am not suggesting revenge for the dead victims. Revenue is not the basis of our judicial and correctional systems. Revenue does not bring the victims back. However, weither can we turn a blind eye to such horrible crimes. The numbers of mass or serial murders are growing. In the United States, over 120 serial murderers are now in prison. Many have killed hundreds of innocent people in the course of their lives. Yet they feel little or no remorse for the taking of another person's life.
The notorious Henry Lee Lucas from the State of Virginia, who claims to have murdered over 360 people in 32 years, says, "Once I've done a crime, I just forget it. I go from crime to crime". Lucas' partner, Otis Elwood Toole, also shows no remorse. "I think of killing like smoking a cigarette, like another habit", he said.
We have a responsibility to break that habit of our mass and serial murderers. It is a habit that knows no economic, social or geographical barriers. While the United States is particularly plagued by most of the known serial murderers, here in Canada we too have experienced the trauma and terror that these murderers induce.
Our nation's attention has been riveted to the Clifford Olson case. However, that is just one example. We do not want a

December 13, 1984
Execution of Mass Murderers Act repeat of that horror to happen to any Canadians in the future. Those terrible events are ongoing in the hearts of the victims' families. Our main objective is to provide a deterrent to those considering murdering many times over.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize yet again that it is our responsibility to provide a measure which will give the potential mass murderer reason to re-think his proposed course of action. It is not a matter of revenge but a matter of being responsible and providing justice for our society. To provide for the capital punishment of murderers, I support this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, the Bill presented by my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Taylor) touches on a fundamental issue. However, I do not want to use the precious time of this House to discuss the basic issue of this Bill, which is an attempt to reintroduce capital punishment into the Canadian penal system. We are all aware of the significance of this matter and the interest it generates. I am convinced that my colleague is proposing this legislation with the conviction that capital punishment is necessary for the welfare of Canadians. 1 do not intend to discuss the logic of this conviction. However, I do have an opinion on the subject.
Like other Canadians, the events of the past months have made me reflect on the issue of capital punishment. The Prime Minister has already indicated there will be a debate on the subject at some time during this session. The debate, to be followed by a free vote by all Members of the House, makes us aware of the fundamental significance of our own individual opinions on the subject, but I do not intend to discuss with you my own opinion nor the arguments in favour or against reinstatement of capital punishment in Canada. I do not think this is the appropriate time to do so.
Mr. Speaker, I may have said this before, but in any case, the Prime Minister gave Canadians the assurance that this difficult subject would be debated in the House at some time during this session of Parliament. The debate will probably be long and heated, as were all debates on this issue, including the debate in July 1976, when capital punishment was removed from the Criminal Code of Canada. No doubt every aspect will be examined and analyzed in detail, with statistics attached. No doubt the results of this debate, whether to reinstate capital punishment or to maintain its removal from the Criminal Code, a will be milestone in the evolution of Canada's penal system. However, and that is where I object to the Bill presented by my hon. friend, all the aspects and implications of the issue of capital punishment should be studied and debated, not just one particular case to which it could be applied. In other words, we shall have to consider the humanitarian as well as the preventive or reparatory aspects of such punishment and the impact it will have on Canadian society and on Canada's image abroad.
I feel that because of its fragmentary and superficial nature, the Bill presented by my hon. friend does not lend itself to this kind of debate and is therefore inopportune.
Mr. Speaker, that is not my only objection to the Bill now before the House. I am also firmly opposed to the Bill on substantive grounds because I feel it is inadequate in what it is trying to accomplish. It is enough to analyze the Bill's various paragraphs to see what kind of problems it raises. Mr. Speaker, the Bill is inadequate throughout because it deals with the complex issue of capital punishment in a few minor considerations, a preamble and a few clauses that lack substance.
Let us look at the preamble. The Bill deals only with one specific aspect of the issue, namely the death penalty for mass murderers. In my opinion, the scope of the Bill is too narrow; it does not meet the stated purpose explicitly described in the whereas clauses of the preamble, which is to relieve Canadians of their fears in general, lessen the grief and remove the anguish of the families of the victims of such criminals.
Murderers convicted of killing at least 10 people certainly deserve a particularly severe penalty and unequivocal condemnation of their actions which I would describe as savage. There is no question about the panic caused by a series of murders in a community or the anguish suffered by the families of victims. However, by what logic would these murderers be condemned to death while others who have committed actions just as monstrous, such as nine murders, would be spared?
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member would probably reply that you have to start somewhere and that is not because it is impossible to condemn to death all murderers that none of them should be condemned. While I do not question his sincerity in the least, I must seriously wonder as to the timeliness of proceeding as he suggests by legislating on a piecemeal basis. By proceeding in specific cases, would we not be doing in a roundabout and virtually secret way what we have promised to debate publicly?
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, if the death penalty must one day be reinstated in Canadian criminal law, this must be done following a comprehensive debate and discussion and not by what I would call a roundabout way. To do otherwise would be unworthy of this House, whatever the personal beliefs of every one of us on this matter. It would be unworthy because we would be depriving the Canadian people and ourselves of the comprehensive debate that the subject deserves, and also because, by acting in this way, we would risk developing a body of law without any guidelines, made up of individual cases and exceptions.
However, this is not the only problem with the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member. Indeed, clause 3 of this Bill sets deadlines for the execution of a mass murderer, which would be 90 days after the coming into effect of the legislation or 90 days after expiry of any time for appeal after the tenth guilty verdict is delivered, whether or not the murderer has exerciced his right to appeal or not. In other words, the Hon. Member
December 13, 1984

for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) is suggesting that the hanging take place before the appeal is heard. Let us hang him right away and we shall see later if he really murdered ten people! In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, he disregards the right of appeal, which is fundamental in our penal system and which can normally be exercised up to the highest Court in the land, that is the Supreme Court of Canada. Moreover, the Hon. Member is ignoring completely the historical right of all those condemned to death to petition for a reprieve or a commutation of sentence. During this week when we are celebrating the 36th anniversary of the International Bill of Rights, it is ironic that this House should be asked to consider a Bill which deliberately goes against some of the most basic rights guaranteed by this charter and by various other international instruments, including the International Covenant on Civil Political Rights.
I need not to remind this House that Canada has played an active role in the formulation and the adoption of these instruments. By passing such a Bill, we would be repudiating all the international commitments made by Canada in the field of human rights. For instance, as recently as last May, at a meeting of the Economic and Social Council of the United Nations, Canada approved a resolution containing provisions which reasserted the commitment already made in the International Bill of Rights and the Covenant. Anyone condemned to death has the right to petition for a reprieve or a commutation of sentence, and this can be granted to anyone condemned to death. The capital penalty will not be applied if there is an appeals procedure or any other procedure or power to obtain a reprieve or a commutation of a death sentence.
We are all aware that those provisions are not operative in Canada, but are we not morally required to honour our international commitments, inasmuch as Canada has for so long played the role of a supporter and promoter of human rights in the world?
Also, under our Common Law, anyone sentenced to death is entitled to clemency and pardon. Such executive clemency is a royal prerogative and an integral part of our Canadian judicial traditions that are confirmed in our Criminal Code.
Mr. Speaker, it is my view that the enactment of my hon. colleague's Bill would place Canada on an equal footing with some nations that ignore human rights and profess that international commitments are of no value, even moral even symbolic. Surely this House has no desire to opt for the road proposed by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor).
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, it is Clause 5 of the legislation that I would like to discuss, the Clause under which my hon. colleague proposes to bypass the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms enacted less than three years ago for the purpose of entrenching for Canadians, under the Constitution itself, the most basic rights, the most essential to the survival and growth of democracy.
Execution of Mass Murderers Act
My hon. colleague proposes to use the procedure provided for in Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the "notwithstanding" Section under which the Parliament of Canada or a Legislative Assembly can specify that an Act shall operate notwithstanding the Charter. So my hon. colleague would have us bypass the Charter, ignore those basic guarantees that all Canadians are supposed to enjoy. But what are those specific guarantees he proposes to bypass? The one in Section 7, the right to life, liberty and security, not to be infringed upon except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice? The one in Section 12, the protection against cruel and irrelevant treatment and penalties? And finally, the one in Section 11, the right to the benefits of the lesser punishment if the punishment has been changed between the time of commission and the time of the sentencing?
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt in my mind that it is in all good faith and quite within the law that my hon. colleague, by way of Clause 5 of the Bill, tries to bypass those provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. But I have serious doubts as to whether we should do so. Since April 1982, when the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms came into force, the Canadian people have been convinced that their rights are protected. They are assured that there is a mechanism which guarantees that their rights are safeguarded.
It is my view that it would be unworthy of the Parliament of Canada to use Section 33 in order to keep the Charter away from a debate in which its application is so basic. Bypassing the Canadian Charter under such circumstances would downgrade it to the level of an ordinary piece of legislation, rob it of all its character of a constitutional, basic and supreme statute.
I indicated earlier that this legislation was not appropriate by reason especially of the commitment made by our Leader to refer the question to the House for scrutiny and propose a free vote on it. The Prime Minister renewed that commitment in this House on December 3, in answer to the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan). Is our Leader's commitment not enough for my colleague from Bow River (Mr. Taylor)?
Also, without being an expert on parliamentary procedure, I do not feel a Private Member's Bill is the right avenue for debating a matter of public interest, as it is in my view.
Indeed, it seems to me that the public interest is at stake here, and that the Hon. Member's Bill is not under the circumstances the most appropriate way of raising the issue of capital punishment.
Although we realize that capital punishment is of interest to the public, and that the Government is very sensitive to the expressed concerns of Canadians, it is therefore my view that introducing this legislation is not the proper procedure for debating the issue.

December 13, 1984
Adjournment Debate

Mr. Speaker, I deeply regret that the time left to debate Bill C-209 is so very short. I am sure that if the subject of the way to deal with those who commit capital offences is ever debated in the House, it will be debated at very great length because of the gravity and seriousness of the subject. Doubtless, many of us will want to scrutinize carefully every aspect of it because of its importance to us.
1 would first like to express my appreciation to the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) for the views which he expressed. I identify with those views. I would also like to express my appreciation to the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) for his discussion of the specifics of this particular Bill, some of his concerns about it, and why it might not be the appropriate way in which to approach the much more complex and underlying issue of capital punishment.
I believe we must seriously address ourselves to the victims who suffer one murder, never mind the cases of the perpetrators of mass murders. What are we going to do to take care of the tremendous trauma, suffering and sorrow which takes place with the death of one person? I hope this Government will address itself in a better way than the previous Government might have addressed itself to this problem. We must address the concerns of the victims of crime. I know that the last Government began to address this problem, and I hope that trend will continue in the future.
I would also like to express my concern about the entire matter which deals with mass murderers, not only the mass murderers of individuals who are selected one by one, but the whole issue of terrorism. When this subject arises in the House again I would like to have the opportunity to speak about this tragic concern.

subtopic: FISHERIES-GEORGES BANK BOUNDARY DECISION-POSSIBLE STATES REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER NEGOTIATE MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT
FISHERIES-GEORGES BANK BOUNDARY DECISION-POSSIBLE STATES REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER NEGOTIATE MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past few days I have brought to the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and this House my concern regarding the successful implementation of the Georges Bank decision which has handed down by the World Court. The reasons for my concern were genuine because relations between Canadian and American fishermen have not always been good, and there has been no indication that those relations will improve with the Georges Bank decision. Because of the request made by the administration of the United States Government to have implementation of the decision delayed for a one-year moratorium, it has become even more important that negotiations on the decision be started immediately.
There is no doubt that the Prime Minister and Hon. Members of the House are aware of the long history of the Georges Bank dispute. Negotiations between the American and Canadian fishermen began in the early 1970s when a compromise on fishing rights was reached. However, eventually it was rejected by the New England fishermen. Canadian-American negotiations were continued through the late 1970s with Canada's Mr. Cadieux and the U.S. negotiator, Mr. Cutler, and an agreement was reached. But with the change of the American Government at that time, the agreement was not implemented. Therefore, when our countries could not come to any agreement, both countries agreed to put the case before the international Court of Justice. Although decisions made by the World Court are not binding, both countries agreed at that time that they would abide by the World Court decision.
As we are all now aware, the decision was reached and handed down. The decision did not give Canada everything she asked for, nor did it give the United States everything it asked for. However, I believe, and I feel most Canadians believe, that it was a good compromise because the smaller area which was given to Canada-about half of what was originally asked for-happens to be, a richer density of scallop fishery. I believe that Canadian fishermen can learn to live with that decision.
What is important now, however, Mr. Speaker, is the immediate implementation of that decision in order that Canadian fisheries management systems may go into effect, especially, of course, in the scallop beds, in order to ensure a healthy and productive fishery in the future.
Just the other day we had an official request by the American administration for the imposition of a moratorium. I posed the question the other day to the Minister and to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and I was pleased with the reply of the Secretary of State for External Affairs that they were not interested in a moratorium. This is something about which we should all be extremely concerned because it is time we get on with the job of good solid fisheries management of the Georges Bank, which will not only benefit Canadian fishermen, but will also benefit American fishermen.
The Canadian record of fisheries management has been very good in the context of world management of fisheries. Our biologists and scientists recognize the need for quality improvement to enhance the species. We cannot take everything; there has to be some stock left so the species will continue to thrive and be economically feasible for fishing. Of course we use the basic principle of size limits on shellfish and
December 13, 1984

age limits for groundfish and the pelagic species. That is basically good solid management.
I am also concerned, Mr. Speaker, that just lately the International Trade Commission fact finding report, concluded on Wednesday, fully supports the U.S. claims that Canadian fish imports are injuring the New England markets. I am a little bit skeptical of that because it seems to be a lever over the heads of Canadians. I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) and the Prime Minister-at the highest levels, that is my concern-assure Canadian fishermen that they get their rightful share and proper management. Unfortunately ground-fish and pelagic fish will not fly the flags of Canada nor the flags of the United States; they are trans-boundary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stewart Mclnnes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: FISHERIES-GEORGES BANK BOUNDARY DECISION-POSSIBLE STATES REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER NEGOTIATE MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) for raising this matter. The Government does not significantly differ from the position he stated, but for the record I think it would be appropriate that I review the history of this situation.
On October 12, the International Court of Justice established the Maritime boundary in the Gulf of Maine. That is the boundary, it is final and not in dispute. Indeed, in this House On December 5, in response to a question from the Hon. Member, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) put the position of the Government of Canada very clearly.
Before going to the International Court of Justice, you will recall, Mr. Speaker, that Canada had negotiated and signed a treaty with the Americans which would have provided for reciprocal fishing rights and joint management of certain Gulf of Maine stocks, so that both countries would have experienced minimum changes to their established fishing patterns wherever the International Court of Justice might place the Maritime boundary between them. In the end this agreement was rejected by the U.S. Senate. The Americans have now proposed that both countries continue fishing as before in the former disputed area for a period of one year while they assess the implications of the decision and develop their position for such further negotiations as might be necessary in respect of East Coast fishery resources.
An official proposal on these lines was received from the U.S. Government on December 7. It acknowledges the final and binding character of the boundary fixed by the International Court of Justice. The Ministers concerned have not yet had an opportunity to finalize a formal response. However, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has stated publicly that we do not envision agreeing to the proposal. We have serious doubts about it.
One of our concerns is to avoid a return, however temporary, to a situation where unrestrained fishing might again threaten the living resources of the Gulf of Maine area. Our primary objective is to get on with managing the resource in a
Adjournment Debate
manner that will maintain it and, if possible, let it return to previous levels so that we can protect the jobs of Canadians involved in the fishing industry.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans scientists are working on an analysis of the resources in the Canadian zone in close consultation with the industry. When this analysis is completed, and only then, will we be in a position to determine precisely what we need to do to manage our resources and what we need in the way of co-operation from the Americans.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-PROVISION OF FUNDS TO CREATE JOBS. (B) SOURCE OF FUNDING
EMPLOYMENT-PROVISION OF FUNDS TO CREATE JOBS. (B) SOURCE OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today as a result of a question I put to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on November 29 with regard to certain statements, or musings perhaps, by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) about the money allocated for job creation.
In committee, the Minister indicated that this was not new money. The $1 billion which the Government so flagrantly used in debate and in the scrums with the various press people was implied to be new money for job creation programs. Unfortunately, on questioning the Prime Minister he seemed to indicate that he was not at all certain. That is how it appeared to me. The Government, in its economic statement, released by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), said there is a $1 billion budgetary allocation for job creation programs in Canada. The Minister of Employment and Immigration has now reneged and said that it is not new money but reallocated money. Therefore there are no new funds for direct job creation programs by the Government of Canada.
Much more important, the Government, which was elected with a massive majority on September 4, has reneged on its promises to the Canadian people. It has refused young people an opportunity to enjoy a meaningful life in the years ahead as a result of reneging on its promises. It has disallowed certain moneys under unemployment insurance. It has disallowed the entitlements that older workers in this country possessed up until this time, by cutting them off as well.
When it comes to direct job creation programs, the Conservative Party and its caucus of sheep have done absolutely nothing. They have reneged in the face of concrete fact which suggests beyond a shadow of a doubt that there is need in this country for moneys coming from the Government of Canada to create jobs.
What better example than the Canada Winter Works Program. There is $250 million budgeted for 1984-85. But what is the demand on that money? The demands are unequivocally six times that amount of money.
What do we get from the Prime Minister-this jokester, this man who stands in the House of Commons and laughs at the unemployment in this country? We have nothing but platitudes from him and from the Minister. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) is the real culprit

December 13, 1984
Adjournment Debate
in this. In fact, he is the minister of finance and the one who is setting the policies for the Government.
There is no new money for the unemployed in this country. Not only am I ashamed of the Government, I am ashamed of the caucus Members, those sheep over there and on the ends over here who have done nothing other than quote the Conservative rhetoric that emanates from the United States. They say that foreign investment will be the cure; foreign investment will be the cure for job creation in Canada. But the Minister responsible and the Minister of Employment and Immigration have refused to place on the table in the House of Commons the impact studies which will indicate to Canadians as well as the House how many jobs will be lost as a result of Investment Canada.
The Government is bankrupt of ideas. It is turning back the clock in regard to job opportunities for young people. There are 900,000 young Canadians without employment. What does the Government do? We not only get platitudes from the Prime Minister but from all the front benches.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has echoed in the Chamber and outside the Chamber that the unemployed are not looking hard enough for jobs. Where are the jobs, I ask the Parliamentary Secretary. Why are you not putting more money into Canada Works? Why are you not putting more money in a first chance program for young people? Why are you singling out the unemployed in this country to decrease the deficit of this country? Where is the compassion that you promised during the election campaign?
With great respect, I suggest that this Government is a vaudeville act. Act one was during the election. Now we are into act two. Scene three, if I may add, Mr. Speaker, will come when the Minister of Finance places before this House a budget which I suggest, if it does not address the problems of the unemployed, we in this Party will fight tooth and nail to make sure that the unemployed workers, the young people, will have an opportunity that they deserve. They deserve to have a meaningful life in this century.
This Government is bankrupt of ideas. Its cure is to throw rhetoric at the problems. I for one will not stand in this Chamber and take it sitting down. It is time for the Parliamentary Secretary or the spokesperson for the Conservative Party to stand in his place and tell Canadians just how wrong the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion is, how wrong the real culprit is, the Minister of Finance, and how wrong the Prime Minister is. They have to do something and they ought to do it now for those individuals who are unemployed.
Finally, if I can conclude with a brief remark, Mr. Speaker, this Govenrment has singled out the older workers. Not only has it done nothing for the younger workers and the unemployed, but it has done nothing for the older workers who are ready for retirement and who will be slashed by this ruthless Government. Shame on this Government.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-PROVISION OF FUNDS TO CREATE JOBS. (B) SOURCE OF FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Hudon), I am pleased to enlighten and reassure the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall). I should imagine that, in the mind of the Hon. Member of the Official Opposition, there would be only one way to solve the problem-higher taxes or a larger deficit. That is certainly not how this government sees it.

The new programs will be the subject of wide-ranging consultations between the various levels of government and with the parties involved in the private sector, that is management and unions. With these new initiatives, the unemployed will be offered many real opportunities to make a useful and productive contribution to Canadian society.

subtopic: FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT-REPORTED IMPORTATION OF DRUGS BY SOVIET ATHLETES
FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT-REPORTED IMPORTATION OF DRUGS BY SOVIET ATHLETES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday December 7, I asked the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelenik) the following question:
Will the Hon. Minister cither confirm or deny that three Soviet athletes have been charged with bringing drugs into the country?
December 13, 1984

The Hon. Minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the Hon. Member for his question. I have been informed that three Soviet weightlifters were indeed detained at Mirabel International Airport last evening. They were found to have in their possession restricted drugs, contrary to the provisions of the Canadian Food and Drugs Act. The matter is now in the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and, therefore, I am not in a position to make any further statements.
I have been advised that the three Soviets have been charged with bringing into Canada drugs which are illegal under the Food and Drugs Act. Of course the court will deal with the charges in due course.
1 am concerned about the matter because it is illegal. People coming into Canada who bring in illegal drugs are not only breaking the laws of our land but are showing a disrespect for our laws and our traditions. In sport there have been times when people have drugged themselves in order to be more alert or to build bigger muscles. Others have given drugs to opponents in order to slow them down or dull their senses. The use of drugs in sport is completely contrary to the high ideals we Canadians place on athletic competition.
Probably the worst aspect of this whole deal is the example which is being given to the boys and girls and the young men and women who are athletically inclined in Canada. We hold our sportsmen in high repute. We pay large salaries to our baseball players, our hockey players, et cetera; sometimes even larger than is paid to the Prime Minister of Canada. We honour these athletes. Boys and girls look up to them. When athletes come into a country, they come as honoured guests to take part in tournaments or contests. Our athletes have a tremendous responsibility to make sure that they build their bodies with good food, not drugs; that they get proper sleep; that they get proper exercise; that they set an example of wholesome living, because what they do will have a very real effect upon hundreds of boys and girls who are growing up.
Drugs have many uses. There are drugs which relieve pain. At this very moment we have a Bill before the House which, if passed, will permit the use of heroine to relieve the tremendous pain that is suffered by those with cancer. In my view this is a proper use of drugs. We have drugs which are used for so-called recreational purposes, to take people on a "trip" to make them forget their troubles. Hon. Members will recall that the LeDain commission in 1972, which was commissioned to inquire into the non-medical use of drugs, concluded that "there is as yet no evidence of serious long-term effects from use at current levels of consumption of this drug in North America".
That was in 1972, but by 1981 many prominent authorities on the subject deemed that such an opinion was wrong. Dr. Powelson said in 1967 that "this particular drug is harmless", but by 1974 the same doctor admitted the following:
-in five years 1 knew I was totally wrong . . . medical research groups, after a generation of neglect, began to attribute long-range ill effects to the use of this particular drug.
There are those today who are advocating the use of drugs for relaxation, so-called "trips". When athletes use such drugs, they are betraying the young people who look up to them, and are gradually reducing their own stamina and strength.
Adjournment Debate
There are other drugs which are used to relax muscles or to build muscles or to slow muscles down. Such drugs may be used before a contest so a fighter will not feel pain. Other drugs may be used to superficially keep him alert. Or, such drugs may be used for ulterior purposes by giving them to others to slow them down, to tighten up their muscles, et cetera. There is one good rule to follow; athletes do not need a crutch, and drugs are crutches. They do not need a crutch to build strong bodies. They need good food, good sleep, sound living, wholesome exercise.
I view with disdain the fact that athletes from Russia had the gall to come into Canada and bring with them drugs which they knew to be illegal under the laws of our country.
Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur
Sport)): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise in the House today to elaborate on the matter raised by my friend, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), regarding the infraction committed by not three but two Soviet athletes upon their arrival in Canada last week. I congratulate the Hon. Member for bringing this very important subject matter to the attention of the House.
The athletes were indeed charged under Article 15 of the Food and Drug Act after tests of the capsules identified their substance as illegal under the Act. I must state that 1 am satisfied that the laws of Canada were dealt with efficiently and fairly at that time from a legal standpoint. However, as Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, I cannot and will not condone such an obvious violation, not only in respect of the laws of our country, but the rules of sport and the spirit of fair competition.
On the premise that the use of drugs which artificially enhance performance is harmful to health, ethically wrong and ultimately a threat to high performance sport, Sport Canada has shown initiative in developing a policy to eradicate the use of such drugs.
The competition in question, however, was conducted under the rules and regulations of the International Weightlifting Federation which does not have in its regulations any sanctions or penalties for the possession of a banned doping substance. As a result, the two athletes in question could not be prohibited from competing, as Would have been my hope.
Notwithstanding these circumstances, I initiated discussions with Mr. Gotfield Schodl, President, and Dr. Tamas Ajan, General Secretary, of the IWF. I am pleased to announce that I received assurances from both of these officials that they will undertake the following action. First, the IWF will address the specifics of this incident at the earliest opportunity. Second, a one year suspension against the two weightlifters will be recommended by the officials. Third, the IWF will discuss the adoption of sanctions and penalties for the possession of banned doping substances as well as the use of them. I further requested that Canada be permitted to conduct dope testing at this competition using our International Olympic Committee's accredited laboratory in Montreal.

December 13, 1984
Adjournment Debate
Once again, I must state that this Government is unequivocally opposed to drug use in sport. To this end, our policy mandates every national sport organization to develop a plan to eradicate improper drug use, as well as suspensions for any athlete who uses, possesses or has been convicted of a drug offence in this country or elsewhere. We cannot achieve this in isolation. I am therefore committed to initiating international co-operation to solve this important problem. To this end, I am
contacting my international counterparts with a view to eventually abolishing the use of drugs in amateur sport, not only in Canada, but around the world.
